title: India | RBI Cybersecurity, Information Security and Data Protection
tagline: Spot phishing, guard access and customer data, report incidents to RBI within six hours and secure digital payments under RBI's 2026 Directions.
sectors: Foreign banks operating branches in India
IT, security operations and technology vendors serving banks
description:
This quest teaches the Reserve Bank of India's cybersecurity rules for commercial banks. It is based on the **RBI (Commercial Banks – Cybersecurity, Technology: Risk, Resilience and Assurance Framework) Directions, 2026** and the **RBI (Commercial Banks – Digital Payment Security Controls) Directions, 2026**, both issued on 31 July 2026 and effective on issue, with the secrecy rule in the **KYC Directions, 2025** and the **Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023** in general terms.

RBI requires cybersecurity awareness for every new recruit, annual training for lower and middle management, annual training for all Board members and senior management, targeted training for key executive, operational and security roles, specialised training for staff who handle cyber incidents, and periodic checks of staff awareness. This quest is built for those audiences.

In five stages you join the CISO's office of a fictional bank: the rulebook and governance, phishing and social engineering, access and customer data, incident response and DAKSH reporting, and digital payment security with Board oversight, illustrated by real RBI enforcement actions.

The quest builds knowledge and does not replace your bank's own information security policies, procedures or instructions from your CISO's office; always follow them and the latest RBI text.
audience: All staff of commercial banks in India, including new recruits who must complete cybersecurity awareness
Lower and middle managers who need annual cybersecurity training under RBI's 2026 Directions
Board members, senior management and members of the IT Strategy, IT Steering and Information Security Committees
Staff of the CISO's office, security operations centre and incident response team
Digital banking, payments, branch and contact-centre staff who handle customer credentials and fraud reports
Vendor and partner staff who use the bank's information assets
outcomes: Explain who RBI's 2026 cybersecurity Directions apply to and the roles of the Board, ITSC, ISC, CISO and Head of IT
Recognise phishing, vishing, spoofing and other social engineering and report them to the incident team at once
Apply need-based access, least privilege, multi-factor authentication, removable media and data leak prevention rules
Keep customer information secret and handle personal data with the care the KYC Directions and the DPDP Act expect
Follow the incident response chain, including reporting to RBI on DAKSH within six hours and notifying CERT-In
Describe the digital payment controls, awareness duties and Board oversight that RBI inspectors will test

quest.name: The Six-Hour Shield
quest.premise: You have just joined the CISO's office at Godavari Harbour Bank, a fictional commercial bank headquartered in Bengaluru with branches across India, as its Information Security Awareness Officer. RBI's new 2026 Directions are in force, a phishing wave is hitting staff and customers, and the clock on incident reporting runs in hours, not days. With Nandini, Rohan, Zoya, Joseph and Anil, clear five stages, then face the final boss: the RBI IT examiner's exam.

sessions.title: The Rulebook: RBI's 2026 Cybersecurity Directions and Who Owns What
sessions.summary: Which banks RBI's 2026 cybersecurity Directions cover, how the Board, the IT Strategy Committee, the Information Security Committee, the CISO and the Head of IT share the work, and who must be trained, and when.
objectives: Identify the banks covered by the 2026 Cybersecurity Directions and what they replaced
Describe the roles of the Board, ITSC, IT Steering Committee, ISC, Head of IT and CISO
Explain why the CISO must stay independent of the Head of IT and of business targets
State the awareness and training duties for new recruits, managers, key roles, the Board and senior management

cards.title: Day one in the CISO's office
cards.setting: Office of the CISO, Godavari Harbour Bank head office, MG Road, Bengaluru. 9:00 am.

lines.text: You have just joined Godavari Harbour Bank, a fictional commercial bank with branches across India, as its Information Security Awareness Officer.
Welcome! I'm Nandini Rao, the CISO. Your timing is perfect: RBI issued new cybersecurity Directions for commercial banks on 31 July 2026, and they took effect the same day.
Zoya from the Lucknow branch, on video. Three of my staff got a mail this morning 'from IT' asking them to re-enter their passwords. One clicked.
Rohan, incident response. I've isolated her machine. The clock is already running on our reporting duty.
Joseph Kurian, Head of IT. Before we fight fires, our new joiners still haven't had any cyber awareness session. HR says it's 'optional'.
It isn't optional any more, and it never really was. Stage one is the Rulebook Vault: who RBI's rules cover, who owns what, and who must be trained. Let's open it.

cards.title: One rulebook for cyber and IT risk

scenes.heading: A single framework
scenes.narration: In July 2026 RBI brought its IT governance and cybersecurity instructions for commercial banks into one set of Directions covering governance, risk management, baseline controls, incident response, the security operations centre and IS audit.

scenes.heading: Who it covers
scenes.narration: The Directions apply to commercial banks: banking companies other than small finance, payments and local area banks, plus the nationalised banks and the State Bank of India.

scenes.heading: Foreign bank branches
scenes.narration: For a foreign bank operating through branches, references to the Board mean its controlling or head office. For some chapters, such a bank may comply or explain, if RBI accepts its reasons.

scenes.heading: Out with the old
scenes.narration: The earlier cybersecurity framework and IT governance instructions for commercial banks were repealed. Actions and penalties under the old rules still stand.

scenes.heading: Training is written in
scenes.narration: The Directions make cyber awareness mandatory for every new recruit and require yearly training for managers, the Board and senior management.

cards.title: Who owns cyber risk at the bank
cards.caption: Built from Chapters II and III of the 2026 Cybersecurity Directions.

items.label: Board of Directors
items.detail: Approves IT, information security, cybersecurity, business continuity and incident response policies

items.label: IT Strategy Committee
items.detail: Board-level, at least three directors, chaired by an independent director with IT expertise; meets quarterly

items.label: Senior management and IT Steering Committee
items.detail: Execute the IT strategy and build a culture of IT risk awareness and cyber hygiene

items.label: Information Security Committee
items.detail: Under the ITSC; headed from risk management; approves awareness initiatives

items.label: CISO and Head of IT
items.detail: CISO drives cyber strategy and runs the SOC; Head of IT owns IT controls as first line

items.label: Every employee, vendor and partner
items.detail: Follow security and acceptable-use policies and report anything suspicious

cards.question: Godavari Harbour Bank is a banking company licensed by RBI. Its sister company is a small finance bank. Which of them is covered by the 2026 Cybersecurity Directions for commercial banks?
options: Godavari Harbour Bank only; small finance banks are excluded from the definition of commercial banks used in these Directions
Both of them, because every bank licensed by RBI is a commercial bank for these Directions
Neither of them until RBI sends each bank an individual letter of applicability
cards.explanation: The Directions define commercial banks as banking companies other than small finance, payments and local area banks, plus corresponding new banks and SBI. They took effect on issue, without any individual letter.

cards.title: What the Board and its committees must do
cards.body:
**The Board** approves the strategies and policies for IT, information assets, business continuity, information security and cybersecurity, including incident response and cyber crisis management. It may delegate review to the IT Strategy Committee, but material changes go back to the Board, and the review happens **at least once a year**.

**The ITSC** has at least three directors. Its chair is an independent director with substantial IT expertise (at least seven years managing information systems or leading technology or cyber initiatives). It meets **at least quarterly** and reviews business continuity and DR at least yearly.

**The IT Steering Committee** brings senior IT and business managers together, also at least quarterly.

**The Information Security Committee** works under the ITSC, includes the CISO and is headed by someone from risk management. It approves and monitors security projects and **awareness initiatives** and reviews cyber incidents.

The bank also needs a separate, Board-approved **Cybersecurity Policy**, distinct from its IT and information security policies.

cards.title: Match the role to its duty
cards.prompt: Link each role in the 2026 Directions to one of its duties.

pairs.right: Approves cybersecurity and incident response policies; material changes come back to it
Checks that budgets for IT and cybersecurity match the bank's threats and digital depth
Approves and monitors security awareness initiatives and reviews cyber incidents
First line of defence for IT controls and owner of the DR set-up
Drives cyber strategy, enforces security policies and runs the security operations centre
Creates a culture of IT risk awareness and cyber hygiene across the bank

cards.title: A tidy reorganisation?
cards.setting: Board room, 14th floor. The quarterly ITSC meeting is breaking up.

lines.text: Anil Mehra, chair of the ITSC. Joseph has a proposal to simplify the org chart.
Security and IT should sit together. If Nandini reports to me, approvals move faster. And I'd give her a target for digital account openings so she feels the business pressure.
Faster approvals for whom? If I report to the person whose systems I challenge, my findings can be softened before anyone sees them.
The new Directions have something to say about this. Before we vote, I want your view.

cards.title: Where should the CISO report?
cards.situation: The ITSC is asked to approve Joseph's plan: the CISO would report to the Head of IT and carry a target for digital account openings. Nandini is a General Manager with a strong technical background. What do you advise?

choices.text: Reject the plan: the CISO must not report directly to the Head of IT or carry business targets, and should report to the executive director overseeing risk management.
choices.outcome: Right. The Directions keep the CISO independent of the Head of IT and free of business targets, with a direct line to the executive director (or equivalent) who oversees risk. The CISO is also a permanent invitee to the ITSC and IT Steering Committee.

choices.text: Approve the reporting line but drop the business target, since targets are the only real conflict.
choices.outcome: Only half right. Dropping the target helps, but the Directions also rule out a direct reporting line from the CISO to the Head of IT.

choices.text: Approve the plan if the Board minutes record the reasons, because the Board can override the Directions.
choices.outcome: No. The Board must follow RBI's Directions. Recording reasons does not make a prohibited reporting line acceptable.

choices.text: Approve the plan for six months as a trial and review it at the next ITSC meeting.
choices.outcome: A trial still breaches the Directions for six months, and it weakens the CISO exactly while the new framework beds in.

cards.title: Who must be trained, and how often
cards.caption: Paragraphs 176 and 199-204 of the 2026 Cybersecurity Directions.

items.label: All staff, vendors and partners
items.left: Security policies communicated, plus education on cyber risks

items.label: Key executive, operational and security roles
Board and senior management
items.left: Training on IT and cyber risks and good practice, plus periodic briefings

cards.title: When does the training happen?
cards.prompt: Sort each group by the timing RBI sets in the 2026 Directions.

items.text: A graduate trainee starting at a Lucknow branch
A lateral hire joining the treasury team
A deputy general manager in retail banking
A branch manager in middle management
An independent director on the Board
A SOC analyst who triages cyber incidents
A security administrator who manages firewalls
A core banking database administrator with elevated rights

cards.back: The Board-level IT Strategy Committee: at least three directors, chaired by an independent director with substantial IT expertise, meeting at least quarterly.
The Information Security Committee: works under the ITSC, includes the CISO, is headed from risk management and approves awareness initiatives.
A cyber event that harms the security of an information asset, malicious or not. In RBI's definition it includes IT incidents too.
The everyday security habits senior management must build into the bank's culture: patching, strong passwords, careful clicking, reporting.
The approach for foreign bank branches on certain chapters: they may deviate only if RBI accepts a reasonable justification.
The rules every staff member and service provider must follow when using the bank's information assets, including customer data.

cards.question: Under the 2026 Directions, how often must lower and middle managers receive cybersecurity training?
options: Only once, when they are first promoted into management
Every three years, aligned to the IS audit cycle
Every year
Only after a cyber incident affects their own department
cards.explanation: Paragraph 203 makes awareness programmes mandatory for all new recruits and requires annual training for lower and middle management. Board members and senior management also get annual training under paragraph 204.

cards.title: Real case: Kotak Mahindra Bank, 2024
cards.body:
On **24 April 2024** RBI used its powers under **Section 35A** of the Banking Regulation Act to stop Kotak Mahindra Bank from **onboarding new customers through online and mobile channels** and from **issuing new credit cards**. Existing customers kept their services.

RBI's press release cited its IT examinations for **2022 and 2023** and serious gaps in IT inventory, patch and change management, **user access management**, vendor risk, **data security and data leak prevention**, and business continuity and DR drills. For two years running the bank had been found deficient in **IT risk and information security governance**, and its corrective action plans were inadequate or not sustained. Frequent outages had hurt customers.

On **12 February 2025** RBI lifted the restrictions after remediation and an external audit approved in advance by RBI.

**Lesson:** RBI treats weak cyber governance as a business problem, not just an IT finding.

cards.title: Real case: Union Bank of India, 2019
cards.body:
In **July 2019** RBI imposed a penalty of **₹1 million** on Union Bank of India for not complying with its directions on the cyber security framework in banks.

According to RBI, the examination followed reports that **seven fraudulent messages** with a total value of about **USD 171 million** had been generated through the bank's **SWIFT** system in **2016**. The examination found several deficiencies in the bank's cyber security framework. RBI set the penalty after a show-cause notice and a personal hearing, taking into account the extent of non-compliance and the corrective action taken.

**Lesson:** an incident invites a full look at the framework behind it. Governance, controls and training all come under review.

cards.title: Rulebook Vault: what to carry forward
items: RBI's 2026 Cybersecurity Directions apply to commercial banks, not small finance, payments or local area banks, and took effect on 31 July 2026.
The Board approves cyber policies and reviews them at least yearly; the ITSC and IT Steering Committee meet at least quarterly.
The ISC approves awareness initiatives; the CISO is independent of the Head of IT and has no business targets.
Awareness is mandatory for every new recruit; managers, the Board and senior management are trained every year.
Key roles get targeted training, incident handlers get specialised training, and staff awareness is tested periodically.

cards.prompt: Think of your own role. Which group in RBI's training table do you belong to, when did you last complete cyber training, and who in your bank would know if you had not?

quiz.question: On which date were RBI's Cybersecurity, Technology: Risk, Resilience and Assurance Framework Directions for commercial banks issued, and when did they take effect?
options: Issued on 1 October 2026 and effective after a six-month transition
Issued on 31 July 2026 and effective immediately on issue
Issued on 31 July 2026 and effective from 1 April 2027
Issued on 28 November 2025 and effective on 1 January 2026
quiz.explanation: The Directions are dated 31 July 2026 and state that they come into effect on issue. The October 2026 date is a later update, not the start date.

quiz.question: Which of these institutions falls outside the 2026 Cybersecurity Directions for commercial banks?
options: A nationalised (corresponding new) bank
A private sector banking company with branches across India
A payments bank licensed by RBI
The State Bank of India
quiz.explanation: The definition of commercial banks excludes small finance banks, payments banks and local area banks. SBI, nationalised banks and banking companies are covered.

quiz.question: A foreign bank operates in India through branches. When the Directions refer to 'the Board', whom does that mean for this bank?
options: The RBI regional office supervising the branch
The country head of the Indian branches, acting alone without any reference to the head office abroad
Its controlling or head office that oversees the Indian branch operations
A board of Indian directors the bank must create locally
quiz.explanation: For foreign banks in branch mode, references to the Board are read as references to the controlling or head office overseeing Indian operations.

quiz.question: Godavari Harbour Bank wants to appoint a new ITSC chair. Which candidate meets the Directions?
options: A non-independent director nominated by the largest shareholder, with five years of IT experience
An independent director with eight years of leading technology and cybersecurity projects
An external IT consultant who is not a director but has deep cyber expertise
The managing director, who has led the bank's digital transformation for ten years
quiz.explanation: The ITSC chair must be an independent director with substantial IT expertise, meaning at least seven years managing information systems or leading technology or cyber initiatives. The MD is not independent, five years is too few, and a non-director cannot chair a Board committee.

quiz.question: How often must the IT Strategy Committee meet under the 2026 Directions?
options: At least once every month
At least once every quarter
At least twice a year
Only when the CISO requests a meeting
quiz.explanation: The ITSC must meet at least quarterly. The IT Steering Committee also meets at least quarterly.

quiz.question: Which body approves and monitors the bank's security awareness initiatives?
options: The Audit Committee of the Board, as part of its oversight of the bank's information systems audit
The IT Steering Committee, chaired by the Head of IT
The Information Security Committee, working under the oversight of the ITSC
The HR department, because training belongs to people management
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 23 gives the ISC the job of approving and monitoring information security and cybersecurity projects and security awareness initiatives.

quiz.question: The HR head says cyber awareness for new joiners can be skipped when induction is busy and done 'at the next annual cycle'. What is the correct response?
options: Agree, provided the new joiners sign the acceptable-use policy on day one
Refuse only for staff who will handle customer data
Agree, because RBI only requires annual training for managers
Refuse: awareness is mandatory for all new recruits
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 203 makes cybersecurity awareness mandatory for all new recruits, whatever their role. Signing a policy does not replace the programme.

quiz.question: A bank proposes that its CISO report to the Head of IT and be given a target for digital sales. What does RBI's framework say?
options: Neither: the CISO reports to the risk executive and has no business targets
Both are allowed if the Board approves them and records its reasons in the minutes of the meeting
The reporting line is allowed, but the business target is not
The target is allowed, but the reporting line to the Head of IT is not
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 27 says the CISO must not report directly to the Head of IT and must not be given business targets; paragraph 28 has the CISO report to the executive director or equivalent overseeing risk management.

quiz.question: Which statement about the Board's role in cybersecurity is correct under the 2026 Directions?
options: It approves cyber policies, may delegate their review to the ITSC, and reviews at least yearly
It reviews cyber policies only when RBI asks for a review
It approves the IT budget but leaves cybersecurity policy to management
It may delegate both approval and material amendments of all cyber and incident policies to the CISO's office
quiz.explanation: The Board approves the policies, may delegate their review to the ITSC, approves material amendments itself, and the review happens at least annually.

quiz.question: Why did RBI stop Kotak Mahindra Bank from onboarding new customers online in April 2024?
options: The bank had refused to subscribe to anti-phishing takedown services despite repeated RBI reminders
The bank had failed to file its quarterly cyber incident returns on time
A single data breach exposed the bank's customers on the internet
IT examinations found governance and control gaps the bank had not fixed
quiz.explanation: RBI's press release cited IT examinations for 2022 and 2023, deficiencies in inventory, patching, access, vendor risk, data leak prevention and BCP/DR, and corrective action plans that were not properly met.

sessions.title: Phishing, Vishing and Social Engineering: Staff and Customers
sessions.summary: How phishing, spear phishing, whaling, vishing and rogue apps target bank staff and customers, what technical defences RBI requires, and how you report and educate so the lure fails.
objectives: Recognise the main social engineering attacks named in RBI's 2026 Directions
Describe the mail, anti-phishing and anti-rogue app defences banks must run
Report suspicious messages and behaviour to the incident management team without delay
Explain what RBI expects banks to teach customers about credentials, OTPs, PINs and devices

cards.title: The mail from 'IT Helpdesk'
cards.setting: Hazratganj branch, Lucknow, on a video call with the CISO's office. 11:30 am.

lines.text: The mail looked exactly like ours. Logo, signature, even our helpdesk ticket format. It said passwords expire today and gave a link.
The sender domain was godavari-harb0ur with a zero. A look-alike domain. Our filters caught most copies; three got through.
And now a customer, Mr Tripathi, says someone from 'the bank's fraud team' rang him and asked him to read out an OTP to 'block a suspicious payment'.
Two attacks, one pattern: someone pretending to be trusted, creating urgency, asking for a secret.
My staff are good people. How were they supposed to know?
That is exactly what this stage is for. Welcome to the Lure Lagoon. By the end, your branch will spot the hook before it bites.

scenes.heading: Pretend to be trusted
scenes.narration: RBI defines phishing as a digital form of social engineering that tries to get private or confidential information by posing as a trustworthy party in an electronic message.

scenes.heading: Pick the target
scenes.narration: Spear phishing aims at one person or team using details about them. Whaling aims at senior executives who can approve payments or access.

scenes.heading: Change the channel
scenes.narration: Vishing does the same over a voice call. Reverse phishing tricks customers into calling a fake helpline that the fraudster controls.

scenes.heading: Create urgency
scenes.narration: Every lure pushes you to act now: an expiring password, a blocked account, an urgent payment for the MD. Urgency is the signal to slow down.

scenes.heading: Break the chain
scenes.narration: RBI's Directions require technical defences, staff awareness, customer education and quick reporting. Any one of them can break the chain.

cards.title: Anatomy of a phishing attack on a bank
cards.caption: Reporting at the lure or hook stage gives the incident team the best chance to contain the attack.

items.label: Research
items.detail: The attacker studies the bank, staff names, mail formats and vendors

items.label: Lure
items.detail: A spoofed or look-alike message, call or fake app arrives

items.label: Hook
items.detail: Someone clicks, opens an attachment, installs an app or shares an OTP

items.label: Harvest
items.detail: Credentials, session tokens or remote access are captured

items.label: Exploit
items.detail: The attacker logs in, moves money or plants malware

items.label: Cash out or spread
items.detail: Funds move through mule accounts or the attack spreads inside

cards.question: What makes a message 'phishing' under the definition used in RBI's 2026 Directions?
options: It tries to obtain private or confidential information by pretending to be a trustworthy party in an electronic communication
It contains a computer virus attached as an executable file
It is sent to more than a hundred recipients at the same time
It comes from a sender outside India
cards.explanation: The Directions define phishing as a digital form of social engineering that pretends to be a trustworthy entity to get private or confidential information. Malware, volume and origin are not part of the definition.

cards.title: Red flag or routine?
cards.prompt: Sort each message or request a branch employee might see.

items.text: A mail from a domain that swaps a letter for a number in the bank's name
A caller from 'RBI' asking for your login to 'verify compliance'
An urgent WhatsApp from the 'MD' asking you to buy gift cards today
An attachment type the bank's mail gateway normally blocks, sent via a personal webmail
A request to install a screen-sharing app so 'IT' can fix your PC
A training reminder that asks you to log in through the intranet you always use
A helpdesk ticket update you raised yourself, with no link or attachment
A circular from your regional office shared on the bank's document system

cards.title: Defences: the bank's systems and your habits
cards.caption: Paragraphs 117-120 and 148 of the Cybersecurity Directions and paragraph 37 of the Digital Payment Security Controls Directions.

items.label: Spoofed mail
items.left: Anti-spoofing and DMARC on the bank's mail domains
items.right: Check the sender domain; report look-alikes

items.label: Malicious attachment
items.left: Gateway limits permitted attachment types and scans files
items.right: Never open unexpected files, even from colleagues

items.label: Fake website
items.left: Anti-phishing service finds and takes down phishing sites
items.right: Type the bank's address; never log in from a link

items.label: Rogue app
items.left: Bank monitors app stores and takes down fake apps
items.right: Install only from the bank's official link

items.label: Phone pretext
items.right: Hang up and call back on a known number

cards.title: The MD needs it today
cards.setting: Zoya's cabin, Lucknow branch. 4:40 pm on a Friday.

lines.text: An email arrives from the managing director's name. It is short and polite.
It says he is in a confidential acquisition meeting and needs me to release a vendor payment of ₹48 lakh from a suspense account before 5 pm. No calls, he says, he can't talk.
The display name is right. The address ends in a webmail domain. And our MD has never written to a branch about a payment.
(on the phone) Good instinct. This is business email fraud aimed at someone who can move money. What do you do next?

cards.title: Business email fraud at 4:40 pm
cards.situation: Zoya has an email that appears to come from the MD, asking for an urgent ₹48 lakh payment from a suspense account, with 'no calls'. The deadline is in twenty minutes. What should she do?

choices.text: Not pay; report the email to the incident team through the bank's channel and verify with the MD's office on a known number.
choices.outcome: Best. Verifying through a separate, known channel breaks the pretext, and reporting lets the incident team block the sender, warn others and check whether anyone else got it. RBI's Directions ask banks to encourage exactly this reporting.

choices.text: Reply to the email asking the MD to confirm the payment in writing.
choices.outcome: Replying goes straight back to the fraudster, who will happily confirm. Always verify through a separate channel you already trust.

choices.text: Process half the amount now to show good faith and hold the rest until Monday.
choices.outcome: Any payment rewards the fraud. Money sent to a mule account is very hard to recover.

choices.text: Delete the email and tell no one, since nothing was paid.
choices.outcome: Not paying is right, but deleting loses evidence and the incident team never learns that the MD's name is being spoofed. Others may be targeted next.

cards.title: Name the attack
cards.prompt: Match each social engineering technique to what it looks like at a bank.

pairs.right: A tailored mail to the trade finance team quoting a real customer's LC number
A fake legal notice sent only to the CFO and the MD asking them to open a document
A caller posing as the fraud team asks a customer to read out an OTP
A fake helpline number on a search result that customers call themselves
A sender address that differs from the bank's by one character
A copy of the bank's mobile app on an unofficial site that captures logins

cards.title: Reporting a suspicious message
cards.prompt: Put the steps in the order you should follow when a suspicious mail lands in your inbox.
steps: Do not click links, open attachments or reply
Report it at once through the bank's phishing report button or incident channel
If you clicked or entered details, tell the incident team immediately and say exactly what you did
Follow the incident team's instructions, such as disconnecting the device or resetting credentials
Warn colleagues only in the way the incident team advises, without forwarding the mail

cards.front: 'The bank may call to ask for my OTP to stop a fraud.'
cards.back: Myth. Banks must teach customers the risks of sharing credentials, passwords, OTPs and PINs with anyone. A genuine bank officer never needs them.

cards.front: 'Any app with the bank's logo is safe.'
cards.back: Myth. Banks must help customers get only the authorised app, for example through a link or QR code on the bank's website, and take down rogue apps.

cards.front: 'Screen-sharing apps are fine if the caller is polite.'
cards.back: Myth. RBI asks banks to warn customers about remote access of their devices, a common route for fraud.

cards.front: 'I have to go through safety tips in the bank's app.'
cards.back: Fact. Customers must go through secure usage guidelines, in their preferred language, when onboarding and after major app updates.

cards.front: 'I can report a phishing site to my bank.'
cards.back: Fact. Banks must encourage customers to report phishing mails and sites and must act on those reports.

cards.question: Mr Tripathi tells Zoya a 'fraud team' caller asked for his OTP. Under RBI's Directions, which bank duty does this incident most directly test?
options: Reconciling digital payment transactions within 24 hours of receiving settlement files
Educating customers about the risks of sharing credentials, OTPs and PINs, and acting on reports of phishing
Conducting penetration tests on internet-facing systems every year
Keeping DC and DR sites geographically well separated
cards.explanation: Paragraphs 205-207 of the Cybersecurity Directions and paragraph 64 of the Digital Payment Security Controls Directions require customer education on phishing, vishing and sharing OTPs or PINs, and action on customer reports.

cards.title: The five-second check before you click
cards.body:
- **Sender:** is the domain exactly the bank's, letter for letter?
- **Surprise:** were you expecting this message, link or file?
- **Speed:** is it pushing you to act within minutes?
- **Secret:** is it asking for a password, OTP, PIN or remote access?
- **Switch channel:** if in doubt, verify by calling a number you already know.

If any answer worries you, report it. A false alarm costs a minute; a missed lure can cost crores.

cards.title: Lure Lagoon: what to carry forward
items: Phishing is social engineering by electronic message; vishing, whaling, spear phishing and reverse phishing are its cousins.
Banks must run anti-spoofing mail controls with DMARC, limit attachment types and use anti-phishing and anti-rogue app takedown services.
Staff must be encouraged to report suspicious behaviour to the incident management team, and should report even after a click.
Customers must be taught never to share credentials, OTPs or PINs and to beware of remote access and fake helplines.
Verify unusual requests on a separate, known channel, especially requests to move money.

cards.prompt: Recall the last unexpected message that asked you to click, pay or share something. Which of the five checks would have flagged it, and how would you report it in your bank?

quiz.question: Which pair of mail controls does the 2026 Cybersecurity Directions specifically require banks to implement?
options: Mandatory digital signatures on all customer emails and a complete ban on staff using any webmail
Encryption of every internal email and a ban on all attachments
A weekly manual review of all mail by the CISO and a block on foreign senders
DMARC for the bank's email domains and controls on permitted attachment types
quiz.explanation: Paragraphs 119 and 120 require control of permissible attachment types and a DMARC solution for the bank's email domains, alongside anti-spoofing and look-alike domain protection.

quiz.question: What does RBI require banks to do about phishing websites and rogue applications impersonating them?
options: Rely on customers to find and report such sites
Publish a list of fake sites in a newspaper every quarter
Report each site to the police and wait for a court order before taking any action against it
Subscribe to external anti-phishing and anti-rogue app takedown services
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 148 requires banks to subscribe to anti-phishing and anti-rogue app services from external service providers to identify and take down phishing websites and rogue apps.

quiz.question: A clerk clicked a link in a fake 'password expiry' mail and typed her password, then felt something was wrong. What should she do first?
options: Tell the incident team at once what she clicked and entered
Forward the mail to all colleagues as a warning
Wait to see if anything unusual happens before reporting
Change her password quietly and say nothing, to avoid any disciplinary action against her
quiz.explanation: Speed matters most after a click. RBI asks banks to encourage reporting of suspicious behaviour to the incident team; a quiet password change may not stop a stolen session, and forwarding spreads the lure.

quiz.question: A customer phones the number he found on a search engine for the 'bank helpline' and is asked to install a screen-sharing app. Which threat is this?
options: Spear phishing aimed at a payments team
Reverse phishing combined with a remote access attempt
A distributed denial of service attack
Whaling aimed at a senior executive
quiz.explanation: In reverse phishing, the victim contacts the fraudster through a fake number. The Digital Payment Security Controls Directions require banks to warn customers about reverse phishing and remote access of devices.

quiz.question: What must banks teach customers about credentials under paragraph 207 of the Cybersecurity Directions?
options: The risks of sharing credentials, passwords, OTPs, PINs and other authentication details
How to share OTPs safely, but only with bank staff who first show a valid bank identity card
How to change their PIN every week
How to store passwords safely in a notebook kept at home
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 207 requires banks to educate customers about the risks and consequences of sharing credentials, passwords, OTPs, PINs and other authentication information, with anyone.

quiz.question: An email to only the MD and CFO, made to look like a court summons, asks them to open an attached document. Which term fits best?
options: Tailgating
Reverse phishing
Vishing
Whaling
quiz.explanation: Whaling targets senior executives. RBI's Cyber Crisis Management Plan list includes whaling alongside spear phishing and vishing.

quiz.question: Under the Digital Payment Security Controls Directions, when must customers go through the secure usage guidelines in the bank's payment app?
options: At onboarding and on first use after each app update or major update to the guidelines, with no option to skip
Only if the customer chooses to read them from the help menu
Only after the customer reports a fraud
Only once a year when the bank sends a reminder
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 58 makes the guidelines mandatory, in the customer's preferred language, with confirmation recorded at onboarding and at first use after updates.

quiz.question: Zoya receives an urgent 'MD' email asking for a payment with 'no calls'. Which response best matches RBI's expectations and good practice?
options: Delete the email and tell nobody, since no payment was made
Verify with the MD's office on a known number and report the mail
Reply to the email asking the MD to confirm the payment in writing before releasing it
Pay because the display name is the MD's
quiz.explanation: Verification on a separate, trusted channel defeats the pretext, and reporting lets the incident team respond. Replying reaches the fraudster; deleting loses evidence.

quiz.question: How can a bank help customers avoid downloading a fake mobile banking app, according to the Digital Payment Security Controls Directions?
options: By sending the app file to customers as an SMS attachment
By allowing the app only on phones bought through the bank
By asking customers to email the bank before each download
By publishing the app's checksum, or a direct link or QR code on its website to the authorised app
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 68(5) requires the bank to host the checksum of the current app version, or, where the app is only in app stores, give a direct link or QR code on its website.

quiz.question: A branch receives several customer reports of a phishing site that copies the bank's login page. What does RBI expect the bank to do?
options: Tell customers it is not the bank's responsibility
Take effective remedial action, such as a takedown and customer warnings
Ask customers to report the site to their mobile operator instead
Note the reports in a register and wait for the annual IS audit to review them and decide
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 206 requires banks to encourage customers to report phishing mails and sites and to take effective remedial action when they do.

sessions.title: Access Management and Customer Data: Least Privilege, Secrecy and Leak Prevention
sessions.summary: Who gets access to what and for how long, how privileged and remote access is controlled, why removable media is blocked by default, and how banks keep customer data secret under RBI's Directions and the DPDP Act.
objectives: Apply RBI's access rules: valid business need, least privilege, separation of duties and MFA for privileged users
Explain the controls on teleworking, removable media, mobile devices and vendor staff
Describe the bank's data leak prevention duty across endpoints, networks, servers and vendors
Keep customer information secret and use it only as the KYC Directions and data protection law allow

cards.title: Three keys in the wrong hands
cards.setting: IT Function office, Kochi, on a call with Bengaluru. 10:00 am.

lines.text: Our access review found three things. A contractor who left in June still has an active VPN account. A database administrator has local admin rights on his laptop. And 214 accounts haven't logged in for six months.
Any of those would interest an attacker. The first two would interest an RBI examiner even more.
The phishing at Lucknow stole a branch password. If that user had broad access, we'd be writing a very different incident report.
People say access reviews slow the business down.
Access is a key, not a perk. Stage three is the Keymaster's Gate: who gets which key, for how long, and how we keep customer data where it belongs.

scenes.heading: Only with a business need
scenes.narration: RBI's Directions allow access to information assets only where a valid business need exists. Curiosity, convenience and seniority are not business needs.

scenes.heading: Least privilege
scenes.narration: Give each user the smallest set of rights the job needs, and split duties so no one person can both make and approve a risky change.

scenes.heading: Prove it twice
scenes.narration: Based on risk, banks use two-factor or multi-factor authentication. For privileged users of critical systems and critical activities, MFA is mandatory.

scenes.heading: Watch the powerful
scenes.narration: People with elevated access are closely supervised, and all their activity is logged and reviewed. Abnormal logon patterns are monitored.

scenes.heading: Close the door
scenes.narration: Banks limit invalid logon attempts and deactivate dormant accounts, so forgotten keys cannot be reused.

items.label: Request on business need
items.detail: Access is requested and approved for a defined role and purpose

items.label: Grant least privilege
items.detail: Rights are provisioned centrally, for a set duration if elevated

items.label: Authenticate strongly
items.detail: MFA by risk; mandatory for privileged users of critical systems

items.label: Log and monitor
items.detail: Privileged activity logged and reviewed; odd logons flagged

items.label: Review and recertify
items.detail: Managers confirm access still matches the job

items.label: Revoke and disable
items.detail: Leavers removed at once; dormant accounts deactivated

cards.question: A DBA asks to keep permanent local administrator rights on his laptop 'to save time installing tools'. What do RBI's Directions say?
options: Admin rights on end-user machines are disallowed; rights are given on need-to-know, for a specific duration, through an established process
Allowed for IT staff, because they are trusted users
Allowed if the laptop has antivirus software installed
cards.explanation: Paragraph 108 disallows administrative rights on end-user workstations, PCs and laptops and allows access rights only on a need-to-know basis and for specific durations through an established process.

cards.title: RBI's access, telework and media rules
cards.body:
**User access (paras 104-113):** access only for a valid business need; centralised authentication and authorisation with strong passwords, **least privilege** and **separation of duties**; **mandatory MFA** for privileged users of critical systems and critical activities; privileged access managed, logged and monitored; invalid logons limited; **dormant accounts deactivated**; abnormal logon patterns monitored; credentials and tokens protected from leakage.

**Teleworking (para 114):** secure remote access, **MFA for enterprise access to critical systems**, an inventory of remote-access devices and protection of data shared while working remotely.

**Removable media (paras 121-125):** **not permitted by default** unless authorised for a defined use and duration; media scanned for malware first; limits on what can be copied; secure erasure after use.

**Vendor staff (para 135):** background checks, non-disclosure and security policy compliance agreements for all third-party service providers.

cards.title: Allowed or not allowed?
cards.prompt: Sort each request under RBI's 2026 access and media rules.

items.text: A privileged database login to core banking using password only
Temporary admin rights for a patch window, approved and time-limited
A pen drive, scanned and authorised for a one-day audit data transfer
Keeping a leaver's account active 'in case he comes back'
Remote access to a critical system with MFA from a registered device
A teller who can both create and approve the same beneficiary
A vendor engineer with a background check and signed NDA accessing a server
An unregistered personal laptop connecting to the bank's network

cards.title: The campaign list
cards.setting: Retail sales floor, Bengaluru. Late afternoon.

lines.text: A regional sales manager stops by with a pen drive and a smile.
(on video from Lucknow) He's asking every branch for the same thing: an export of customers with fixed deposits above ₹5 lakh, with mobile numbers.
He wants to hand it to a telemarketing agency to sell an insurance product. He says the customers 'already trust us'.
Trust is exactly what's at stake. Let's think about secrecy, consent, removable media and vendors, all at once.

cards.title: A list on a pen drive
cards.situation: A sales manager asks branches to copy a list of high-value deposit customers with phone numbers to his pen drive, for an outside telemarketing agency to cross-sell insurance. Customers gave their details when opening accounts. What should the branches do?

choices.text: Decline and escalate: account-opening data cannot be used for cross-selling without customers' express permission, removable media is blocked by default and vendor sharing needs proper controls.
choices.outcome: Best. The KYC Directions keep customer information secret and bar using account-opening data for cross-selling without express permission. The Cybersecurity Directions block removable media unless authorised and require data leak prevention at vendors too.

choices.text: Share the list but remove the phone numbers, keeping names and deposit amounts.
choices.outcome: Still a breach. Names with deposit amounts are confidential customer information, and the purpose still lacks the customers' express permission.

choices.text: Share it by encrypted email instead of a pen drive, since encryption solves the risk.
choices.outcome: Encryption protects data in transit, but it doesn't give the bank the right to use the data for cross-selling or to pass it to an agency without consent.

choices.text: Share it if the agency signs an NDA.
choices.outcome: An NDA is a useful vendor control, but it doesn't replace the customer's express permission for a new purpose.

cards.title: Two sources of the confidentiality duty
cards.caption: The DPDP Act is described in general terms only; ask your privacy team for the current duties.

items.label: Core duty
items.left: Keep customer information from the banking relationship secret
items.right: Process digital personal data lawfully and protect it

items.label: Use for other purposes
items.left: No cross-selling with account-opening data without express permission
items.right: Generally needs a lawful basis such as the person's consent

items.label: Security
items.left: Data leak prevention under the Cybersecurity Directions

cards.title: Match the control to its purpose
cards.prompt: Each control comes from RBI's 2026 Directions. Match it to what it protects against.

pairs.right: Loss of sensitive data from endpoints, networks, servers and vendor sites
Customer data on a lost or stolen laptop or phone
Bank data mixing with personal apps on a smartphone
Full account or card numbers exposed in customer messages
Treating all information the same, whatever its sensitivity
Old, unwatched user IDs being reused by attackers

cards.back: A user whose role gives powers in a system well beyond those of most users, such as a database or network administrator.
Each user gets only the rights the job needs, nothing more.
Splitting tasks so one person cannot both make and approve a sensitive action.
Under the DPDP Act, the organisation that decides why and how personal data is processed; a bank is one.
Customers' personal and sensitive data the bank holds as owner and must protect, even at a vendor.
A login that has not been used for a long time and must be deactivated under RBI's rules.

cards.question: Which users must use multi-factor authentication under paragraph 110 of the Cybersecurity Directions, whatever the bank's risk assessment says?
options: Every customer using internet banking for balance enquiries
Only users working from home
Only the CISO and the Head of IT
Privileged users of critical information systems and critical activities
cards.explanation: Paragraph 110 lets banks choose two-factor or multi-factor authentication by risk, but makes MFA mandatory for privileged users of critical systems and critical activities. Telework MFA for critical systems is a separate rule in paragraph 114.

cards.title: Real case: Bank of Bahrain & Kuwait, India Operations, 2022
cards.body:
In **December 2022** RBI imposed a penalty of **₹2.66 crore** on Bank of Bahrain & Kuwait BSC, India Operations, for not complying with its directions on the **Cyber Security Framework in Banks**.

RBI's press release said its IT examination in October 2021 and a cyber incident the bank reported showed the bank had failed to, among other things:

- **disallow administrative rights on endpoints**
- use **multi-factor authentication** for access to critical servers
- control and monitor access to critical servers
- enable **audit logs** and real-time alerts, and run a **security operations centre**
- have a **Cyber Crisis Management Plan**

RBI said these failures let an **unauthorised intrusion go undetected**.

**Lesson:** each missing access control looks small. Together they gave an intruder room to hide.

cards.title: Data protection law in general terms
cards.body:
The **Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023** treats banks as **data fiduciaries** for digital personal data. In broad terms it expects them to use personal data only for lawful purposes, usually with the person's consent or another permitted ground, to protect it with **reasonable security safeguards**, and to tell the **Data Protection Board** and affected people about personal data breaches. The **DPDP Rules, 2025** bring duties into force in phases.

This quest does not state the Act's section numbers or deadlines. Follow your bank's privacy policy and ask your privacy team which duties apply today.

cards.title: Keymaster's Gate: what to carry forward
items: Access only for a valid business need, with least privilege and separation of duties; no admin rights on end-user machines.
MFA is mandatory for privileged users of critical systems and for remote access to critical systems.
Leavers are removed promptly, dormant accounts deactivated, and privileged activity logged and reviewed.
Removable media is blocked by default; data leak prevention covers endpoints, networks, servers and vendors.
Customer information is secret; account-opening data is not used for cross-selling without express permission.

cards.prompt: List the systems you can access today. For each, could you explain the business need to an RBI examiner? Is there any access you no longer need and should ask to remove?

quiz.question: When does paragraph 104 of the Cybersecurity Directions allow a user access to an information asset?
options: Whenever the asset is not classified as critical
Only where a valid business need exists
Whenever the user has finished induction
Whenever the user's manager is senior enough
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 104 is simple: access is allowed only where a valid business need exists. Seniority or training alone do not create a need.

quiz.question: A network administrator works from home and logs into the bank's critical systems through VPN using a password. What is missing under the Directions?
options: Multi-factor authentication for enterprise access to critical systems
A written approval from the Board of Directors for each individual remote session
A ban on all remote work for IT staff
A second VPN from another vendor
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 114 requires MFA for enterprise access to critical systems in teleworking, and paragraph 110 makes MFA mandatory for privileged users of critical systems.

quiz.question: An access review finds 214 user IDs unused for six months. What does RBI's framework expect?
options: Leave them, since unused accounts pose no risk
Deactivate dormant accounts under the bank's controls
Rename them so attackers cannot guess them
Transfer them to the IT team for later use
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 112 requires controls to minimise invalid logons and deactivate dormant accounts, which attackers can otherwise reuse unnoticed.

quiz.question: What is the default rule on removable media such as pen drives in the bank's environment?
options: Permitted if the device is encrypted
Permitted for managers but not for clerks
Not permitted unless specifically authorised for a defined use and duration
Permitted for all staff once scanned by antivirus
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 121 sets a default ban unless media is specifically authorised for a defined use and duration; scanning (para 124) is an additional step, not a replacement.

quiz.question: A sales manager wants account-opening data to cross-sell insurance through an agency. Which RBI rule most directly stops him?
options: The KYC secrecy rule: no such use without express permission
The rule on half-yearly DR drills for critical information systems at the alternate site
The rule that the ITSC meets at least quarterly
The rule requiring DMARC on email domains
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 63 of the KYC Directions keeps customer information secret and bars using account-opening data for cross-selling or other purposes without express permission.

quiz.question: Which statement about the bank's data leak prevention strategy is correct?
options: It applies only when data leaves India
It applies only to customer data, not business data
It only needs to cover the servers in the bank's own primary data centre and its DR site
It covers endpoints, data in transit and stored data, and vendor sites too
quiz.explanation: Paragraphs 51 and 52 require a comprehensive strategy for sensitive business and customer data across endpoints, transmission and storage, online or offline, and similar arrangements at vendor sites.

quiz.question: A teller can both add a new beneficiary to a customer's account and approve the same addition. Which principle is broken?
options: Recovery point objective
Straight through processing
Data classification
Separation of duties
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 109 requires centralised authentication with least privilege and separation of duties, so one person cannot both make and approve a sensitive action.

quiz.question: What must the bank require of all third-party service providers whose staff access its critical assets?
options: Only a letter of comfort from the vendor's CEO
An annual training certificate from CERT-In
Background checks, non-disclosure agreements and security policy compliance agreements
A deposit with the bank equal to the full contract value, refundable at the end of the contract
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 135 mandates background checks, non-disclosure and security policy compliance agreements for all third-party service providers.

quiz.question: In RBI's 2022 action against Bank of Bahrain & Kuwait's India operations, what did RBI say the control failures led to?
options: A ban on issuing new credit cards
A nationwide ATM outage lasting a week
An unauthorised intrusion that went undetected
The loss of the bank's banking licence
quiz.explanation: The press release listed failures such as admin rights on endpoints, no MFA for critical servers, no SOC and no CCMP, which resulted in an unauthorised intrusion going undetected. The penalty was ₹2.66 crore.

quiz.question: Under the Digital Payment Security Controls Directions, how should customer account or card numbers appear in SMS and email messages?
options: Only in email attachments, never in the body
In full, so customers can match them easily
In full, but only in English
Redacted or masked
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 40 requires banks to redact or mask customer information such as account and card numbers in SMS and email, including attachments.

sessions.title: Cyber Incident Response: Six Hours to DAKSH, CERT-In and the Crisis Plan
sessions.summary: How a bank detects, contains, reports and recovers from cyber incidents under RBI's 2026 Directions: the incident response policy, specialised training, DAKSH reporting within six hours, CERT-In, the Cyber Crisis Management Plan, the CSOC and DR drills.
objectives: Describe what the incident response and recovery policy must cover and who needs specialised training
Report a cyber incident to RBI on DAKSH within six hours of detection and notify CERT-In
Explain the four aspects of the Cyber Crisis Management Plan and the CSOC's three levels
Connect incident response to DR drills, recovery objectives and lessons learnt

cards.title: The login that shouldn't exist
cards.setting: Cyber Security Operations Centre, Bengaluru. 10:05 am.

lines.text: SIEM alert. The Lucknow clerk's stolen password was just used from an IP in another state to log into the branch's account-opening module.
So the phish wasn't harmless. Is the session live?
Killed it a minute ago. Account disabled, device quarantined. We confirmed it as a cyber incident at 10:05.
Then the clock started at 10:05. RBI wants this on DAKSH within six hours of detection. Who's drafting?
Shouldn't we wait until we know what they touched? I'd rather not send RBI half a story.
Stage four is the Six-Hour Watchtower. Let's see what 'half a story' means to a regulator.

scenes.heading: Detect
scenes.narration: The CSOC watches logs around the clock. Staff, vendors and customers must also have a clear way to report suspected incidents.

scenes.heading: Contain
scenes.narration: The bank limits the attack by shielding or quarantining affected devices and systems before the damage spreads.

scenes.heading: Report
scenes.narration: RBI requires banks to report cyber incidents on DAKSH, its supervisory monitoring platform, within six hours of detection, and to notify CERT-In proactively.

scenes.heading: Analyse
scenes.narration: The bank analyses severity, impact and root cause, using forensics where needed, then takes corrective and preventive action.

scenes.heading: Communicate
scenes.narration: Clear plans escalate the incident to the Board and senior management and inform customers where required.

scenes.heading: Learn
scenes.narration: Lessons from incidents, tests and drills feed back into the response plans.

cards.title: The Cyber Crisis Management Plan
cards.caption: The CCMP is part of the Board-approved cybersecurity framework and must address these four aspects (paragraphs 192-193).

items.label: Detection
items.detail: Spot intrusions quickly through monitoring, alerts and staff reports

items.label: Containment
items.detail: Isolate affected systems and stop the spread

items.label: Response
items.detail: Act on the threat, report, communicate and coordinate

items.label: Recovery
items.detail: Restore services securely within recovery objectives, then learn

cards.question: Rohan's team confirmed the incident at 10:05 am. By when must Godavari Harbour Bank report it to RBI on DAKSH?
options: By 4:05 pm the same day, within six hours of detection
By 10:05 am the next day, within twenty-four hours
Within seventy-two hours, once forensics are complete
Only after root cause analysis is approved by the ISC
cards.explanation: Paragraph 182 requires reporting within six hours of detection on the DAKSH platform. Analysis continues after the first report; it does not delay it.

cards.title: What the incident response policy must cover
cards.body:
Under paragraph 175 the bank's cyber incident response and recovery policy must address:

- definition, classification and assessment of incidents
- roles of staff **and outsourced staff** who handle incidents
- how **employees, vendors and customers** report incidents
- a clear communication strategy and plan
- containment and timely recovery
- collecting and sharing threat information
- post-incident review
- periodic testing of response plans

Paragraph 176 adds that **personnel handling cyber incidents must receive specialised training**. Response plans must also be ready for scenarios such as ransomware, data destruction and DDoS.

If customers' personal data is involved, data protection law adds its own breach duties. Bring in your privacy team at once.

cards.title: Handling the Lucknow incident
cards.prompt: Put Rohan's actions in the order RBI's framework and good practice suggest.
steps: Validate the alert and confirm it as a cyber incident, noting the time of detection
Contain it: end the session, disable the account and quarantine the device
Report it to RBI on DAKSH within six hours, notify CERT-In and escalate under the communication plan
Analyse severity, impact and root cause, with forensics if needed
Fix the root cause and feed lessons into the response plan

cards.title: The Lucknow incident clock
cards.caption: An illustrative timeline for the quest's fictional incident.

items.label: Phish clicked
items.detail: A clerk enters her password on a look-alike page

items.label: Detected
items.detail: SIEM alert confirmed as a cyber incident; clock starts

items.label: Contained
items.detail: Session killed, account disabled, device quarantined

items.label: Reported
items.detail: Initial report on DAKSH; CERT-In notified

items.label: Six-hour limit
items.detail: Latest time for the DAKSH report

items.label: Root cause
items.detail: Forensics, fixes and lessons learnt

lines.text: We still don't know if any customer records were viewed. If we report now, we may have to correct it later. That looks bad.
We know enough: confirmed unauthorised access to a bank system using a stolen credential.
(on the phone) As ITSC chair, I'd rather explain an update than explain a late report. What does the rule say?
Joseph wants certainty. RBI wants speed. Let's decide.

cards.title: Report now or wait?
cards.situation: It is 11:40 am. The incident was detected at 10:05 am. The team knows a stolen credential was used to access a branch module, but not yet whether customer data was viewed. Joseph wants to wait for forensic results expected tomorrow. What should the bank do?

choices.text: Report on DAKSH now with the facts known, notify CERT-In, and send updates as forensics progress.
choices.outcome: Best. The six-hour limit runs from detection, not from the end of the investigation. An initial report with known facts, followed by updates, meets RBI's rule and keeps the regulator informed.

choices.text: Wait for tomorrow's forensic report so RBI gets one complete, accurate submission.
choices.outcome: This misses the six-hour window. Accuracy matters, but RBI expects timely reporting and allows the bank to add detail later.

choices.text: Report to CERT-In now and to RBI after forensics, since CERT-In is the cyber agency.
choices.outcome: Both are needed. The Directions require reporting to RBI on DAKSH within six hours and proactive notification to CERT-In; one does not replace the other.

choices.text: Report only if forensics confirm that customer data was accessed.
choices.outcome: A cyber incident is reportable whether or not customer data was touched. Waiting for that answer misses the deadline.

cards.title: Who staffs the Cyber Security Operations Centre
cards.caption: Paragraph 221. All CSOC staff, in-house or from a service provider, must be adequately trained (paragraph 223).

items.label: Level 3: advanced analysts
items.detail: Deep packet analysis, IOC collection, forensic evidence, malware reverse engineering

items.label: Level 2: specialists
items.detail: Network, data and endpoint security experts for root cause and corrective action

items.label: Level 1: round-the-clock monitoring
items.detail: Adequately trained staff with product and vendor certifications watching 24x7

cards.title: Whose job is it?
cards.prompt: Sort each incident duty to the people mainly responsible.

items.text: Report a suspicious mail or odd system behaviour at once
Tell the incident team immediately after clicking a bad link
Quarantine affected devices and analyse root cause
Submit the DAKSH report and notify CERT-In
Collect indicators of compromise and preserve evidence
Receive escalations and oversee the response
Approve the cybersecurity framework that includes the CCMP

cards.back: RBI's Advanced Supervisory Monitoring System. Banks report cyber incidents on it within six hours of detection.
The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team. Banks must notify it of cyber incidents proactively, alongside RBI.
The Indian Banks Centre for Analysis of Risks and Threats, set up by IDRBT, where banks may share threat intelligence.
Cyber Crisis Management Plan: part of the Board-approved framework, covering detection, containment, response and recovery.
Recovery Time Objective: how long a system can be in recovery before the business is hurt. The ITSC approves a minimal RTO for critical systems.
Recovery Point Objective: the point in time to which data must be recovered. RBI wants near zero for critical systems.

cards.question: How often must a bank run DR drills for its critical information systems under the 2026 Directions?
options: Once a year, in a test environment only
Every three years, with the IS audit
Only after a major outage
At least every six months, switching to the DR site for at least a full working day
cards.explanation: Paragraph 165 sets DR drills for critical systems at least half-yearly, and paragraph 167 requires running from the DR or alternate site for at least a full working day, beginning to end of day.

cards.title: Real case: Tamilnad Mercantile Bank, 2021
cards.body:
In **May 2021** RBI imposed a penalty of **₹1 crore** on Tamilnad Mercantile Bank for not complying with certain provisions of RBI's **Cyber Security Framework in Banks** directions of 2016.

RBI's press release explained that the bank had **reported a few cyber incidents to RBI in October 2019**. When RBI examined those incident reports, it found non-compliance with the framework. After a show-cause notice, the bank's reply, a personal hearing and further submissions, RBI found the charges substantiated.

**Lesson:** reporting is required and it is right. But an incident report also shows the regulator how well your controls work. The best protection is a framework that holds up when someone looks closely.

cards.title: Real case: Corporation Bank, 2019
cards.body:
In **August 2019** RBI imposed a penalty of **₹1 crore** on Corporation Bank for not complying with its directions on the **Cyber Security Framework in Banks** and on **fraud classification and reporting**.

According to RBI, the case began with a **cyber security incident report** the bank itself submitted, about **fraudulent transactions using a cancelled debit card**. Reviewing that report showed the bank had not complied with both sets of directions. RBI found the charges substantiated after the bank's reply and a personal hearing.

**Lesson:** a cyber incident is often a fraud incident too. Incident response and fraud reporting must work together.

cards.title: Six-Hour Watchtower: what to carry forward
items: The incident response policy covers classification, roles (including outsourced staff), reporting by staff, vendors and customers, communication, recovery and testing.
Staff who handle cyber incidents must get specialised training; CSOC staff must be adequately trained at every level.
Report cyber incidents to RBI on DAKSH within six hours of detection and notify CERT-In proactively; update as facts emerge.
The Board-approved CCMP covers detection, containment, response and recovery, including ransomware, DDoS and phishing.
DR drills for critical systems run at least half-yearly, and lessons from incidents and drills improve the plans.

cards.prompt: If you spotted a cyber incident at 6 pm on a Friday, who exactly would you call, and how would they know the six-hour clock had started? Write down the contact you would use.

quiz.question: Within what time must a commercial bank report a cyber incident to RBI, and where?
options: Within twenty-four hours of detection, by email to the RBI regional office
Within six hours of detection, on the DAKSH platform
Within six hours of the incident starting, through CERT-In's portal
Within seventy-two hours of confirming root cause, on DAKSH
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 182 requires reporting within six hours of detection on DAKSH, RBI's supervisory monitoring system, plus proactive notification to CERT-In.

quiz.question: Which group must receive specialised training under paragraph 176 of the Cybersecurity Directions?
options: Personnel who handle cyber incidents
External auditors of the bank
Branch security guards only
All customers of the bank
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 176 requires specialised training for personnel handling cyber incidents, in addition to the general awareness programme.

quiz.question: Forensic results will take two more days. The incident was detected four hours ago. What should the bank do about reporting to RBI?
options: Report only if customer data turns out to be affected
Wait for the forensic findings so the report to RBI is complete and accurate in one go
Report on DAKSH now with known facts and update RBI later
Report only to CERT-In now and to RBI later
quiz.explanation: The six-hour clock runs from detection. A timely initial report with later updates meets the rule; waiting misses it.

quiz.question: Which four aspects must the Cyber Crisis Management Plan address?
options: Prevention, prosecution, publicity and payment
Planning, procurement, patching and penetration testing
Detection, containment, response and recovery
Identification, investigation, insurance and indemnity
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 193 requires the CCMP to address detection, containment, response and recovery.

quiz.question: Which of these must the incident response policy include under paragraph 175?
options: A list of employees to be dismissed after each incident
A mechanism for employees, vendors and customers to report cyber incidents
A promise never to share threat information about incidents with anyone outside the bank
A rule that only the CISO may speak to staff about incidents
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 175 lists items including a reporting mechanism for employees, vendors and customers, communication plans, containment, threat information sharing, post-incident review and testing.

quiz.question: How is Level 1 of the CSOC described in the 2026 Directions?
options: Monthly review of firewall rules by the Head of IT
Malware reverse engineering and custom scripting by the most senior analysts
Board-level oversight of security operations
Round-the-clock monitoring by trained, certified staff
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 221 describes Level 1 as round-the-clock monitoring, Level 2 as specialists for root cause and correction, and Level 3 as advanced analysts with forensic and reverse-engineering skills.

quiz.question: What does RBI require for DR drills on critical information systems?
options: At least yearly, in a test copy of the production system
Only when the ITSC requests one
At least half-yearly, running from the DR site for at least a full working day
Every two years, during a weekend shutdown
quiz.explanation: Paragraphs 165 and 167 require at least half-yearly drills for critical systems that switch to the DR or alternate site for at least a full working day.

quiz.question: After a confirmed attack, Rohan isolates the affected servers from the network. Which duty does this fulfil?
options: Reporting the incident to CERT-In
Containing the attack by shielding or quarantining affected systems
Testing the DR site
Approving the IS audit policy
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 180 requires banks to contain cyber-attacks by shielding controls or quarantining affected devices and systems.

quiz.question: What triggered RBI's 2021 penalty on Tamilnad Mercantile Bank under the Cyber Security Framework?
options: A newspaper report about a data leak
A customer complaint to the RBI Ombudsman about ATM charges that led to a special inspection
Its own October 2019 incident reports revealed non-compliance
A failed DR drill observed by CERT-In
quiz.explanation: RBI's press release says the bank reported a few cyber incidents in October 2019 and examination of those reports revealed non-compliance, leading to a ₹1 crore penalty in May 2021.

quiz.question: Which organisations' cyber drills does RBI expect banks to take part in periodically and actively?
options: Drills run by the bank's statutory auditor
Drills and simulations run under the aegis of agencies such as CERT-In and IDRBT
Drills run by card networks only
Drills run by foreign central banks
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 188 asks banks to participate periodically and actively in cyber drills and simulations conducted by institutions such as CERT-In and IDRBT.

sessions.title: Digital Payment Security, Board Oversight and RBI Inspection Readiness
sessions.summary: The Digital Payment Security Controls Directions 2026 for apps, internet banking and fraud monitoring, the Board's annual cyber training and oversight, the metrics, testing and IS audit cycle, and how to show RBI's IT examiners that the programme works.
objectives: Apply the main Digital Payment Security Controls: MFA, alerts, failed-login limits, fraud rules and reconciliation
Describe the Board's and senior management's annual training and oversight duties
Recall the review, testing and drill frequencies RBI sets for policies, VA/PT, DR and committees
Prepare evidence that the bank's awareness and training programme meets RBI's Directions

cards.title: The examiners are coming
cards.setting: Board room, Godavari Harbour Bank, Bengaluru. 9:30 am.

lines.text: RBI's IT examination team arrives next month. They'll look at the new Directions, our digital payments and, I'm told, us: the Board.
They will. Every Board member and senior manager needs annual training on IT and cyber risks. Two directors joined in August and haven't had it.
And our mobile app team wants to keep two old versions live for another year because some customers don't update.
Branches are also seeing customers who say they never got an alert when a new beneficiary was added.
Then this is our final stage: the Examiner's Citadel. Let's make sure we can show, not just say, that we comply.

cards.title: The Digital Payment Security Controls Directions

scenes.heading: Board-approved policy
scenes.narration: Each commercial bank needs a Board-approved policy for digital payment products, covering functionality, security and performance. The Board may delegate review to the ITSC, at least once a year.

scenes.heading: Strong authentication
scenes.narration: Electronic payments and fund transfers need multi-factor authentication, unless RBI has relaxed it, and at least one factor must be dynamic or non-replicable, such as an OTP, device binding or a biometric.

scenes.heading: Alerts that mean something
scenes.narration: Customers get MFA and alerts for payments, new or changed beneficiaries, changed account details and new limits. Alerts name the merchant, not just the payment aggregator.

scenes.heading: Fraud rules and trained staff
scenes.narration: Banks set fraud rules for things like transaction velocity and new beneficiaries, and train fraud control staff in tools, investigation and rule setting.

scenes.heading: Safe apps
scenes.narration: Mobile apps are bound to the device, re-authenticate at launch and retire old versions within six months of a new release.

cards.title: Securing a digital payment product
cards.caption: Built from Chapters II and III of the Digital Payment Security Controls Directions, 2026.

items.label: Policy and risk assessment
items.detail: Board-approved policy; risk assessed before launch and regularly after

items.label: Secure by design
items.detail: Threat modelling, secure coding, source code review, VA and PT before go-live

items.label: Strong authentication
items.detail: MFA with a dynamic or non-replicable factor; failed-login limits

items.label: Monitor for fraud
items.detail: Parameterised alerts on velocity, geography, new beneficiaries and more

items.label: Reconcile
items.detail: Reconcile with all stakeholders no later than 24 hours from settlement files

items.label: Protect and educate customers
items.detail: Mandatory safe-usage guidance, alerts, easy fraud marking and grievance routes

cards.question: Which authentication set-up meets paragraph 41 of the Digital Payment Security Controls Directions for a fund transfer in the mobile app?
options: A PIN plus device binding to the customer's registered phone
A password plus the customer's date of birth
A password plus a security question about the customer's first school
A username plus a static PIN printed in the welcome kit
cards.explanation: MFA is required and at least one factor must be dynamic or non-replicable, such as OTP, device binding with SIM, biometrics or hardware tokens. A password, date of birth or static PIN can all be copied.

cards.title: Payment control and its rule
cards.prompt: Match each digital payment control to what the 2026 Directions require.

pairs.right: The bank sets a maximum number of failed attempts, then blocks access and notifies the customer
Sent for debits, credits, beneficiary changes and limit changes, naming the merchant
Real-time or near-real-time, no later than 24 hours from receiving settlement files
Phased out within six months of the newer version's release
Customer notified on multiple channels and can disable a registered device
Customers can flag a transaction as fraudulent in the app for immediate notice to the bank

cards.title: Board oversight and the assurance cycle
cards.body:
**Board and senior management (para 204):** kept aware of evolving threats through periodic briefings, and given **annual training** on IT and cyber risks and good practice.

**CISO (para 28):** places a review of cyber risks and preparedness before the Board, its Risk Management Committee or the ITSC **at least quarterly**.

**Testing (paras 151, 161):** for critical systems and customer-facing DMZ systems, **VA at least every six months and PT at least every 12 months**. Closure of findings goes to the ITSC and ISC at least quarterly.
